scenes.name: Grunge y rock alternativo
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Nevermind de Nirvana (noviembre de 1991) llega al número uno el 11 de enero de 1992 y acaba con el reinado del lite metal. Los medios abrazan a Kurt Cobain y Eddie Vedder, las radios crean formatos «alternativos», la gran emisora de metal de Los Ángeles, KNAC, se vende en 1995 y MTV cancela Headbangers Ball en 1996; hasta Kerrang! se abre a la nueva moda, y los críticos, que crecieron con el rock universitario, ven por fin validado su gusto. El grunge no es metal aunque comparte la guitarra y la voz fuerte: alterna partes duras y suaves, canta el dolor y la desesperación, viste de tienda de segunda mano e identifica a la generación X con los débiles, frente al poder y el placer del metal («Somos pesados, pero no heavy metal», dice Krist Novoselic). Hacia 1998 el alternativo está moribundo.

podcast.title: Mattel's Big Wheel Commercial Appearance (1972)
podcast.body: Around age seven or eight in 1972, Eddie Vedder appeared in a nationally broadcast TV commercial for Mattel's Big Wheel, which ran during Saturday morning cartoons. "One of the kids on the Big Wheel? Eddie Vetter."

podcast.title: Move to Seattle (1991)
podcast.body: During the filming of *Singles* in early 1991, Eddie Vedder had already moved from San Diego to Seattle. At this time, he was "hanging out with his future bandmates," indicating the very early stages of Pearl Jam's formation, before the band's widespread recognition. "As Singles started filling, Pearl Jam had barely been born, although Eddie Vetter had already moved from San Diego to Seattle where he was hanging out with his future bandmates."

podcast.title: Legal Dispute over "Hard Sun" Cover (2010)
podcast.body: Despite not being legally required to ask for permission to cover a song, Eddie Vedder was sued by the original composer, Gordon Peterson, for allegedly not seeking permission and for "eroding the integrity" of the song by changing some lyrics. The case went to court until April 2010, when a judge ruled that Vedder did not materially infringe on Peterson's song. "The case wound its way through the courts until April 2010 when a judge ruled that Eddie did not materially infringe on Peterson's song."

podcast.title: Child Modeling Career (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: Before his fame as a grunge icon, Eddie Vedder had a child modeling career in Chicago, often paraded by his mother through photo shoots and TV commercial auditions. He had a headshot listing his details (Eddie J. Mueller, height 43 inches, weight 38 pounds, size 5, hair light brown, eyes blue) and appeared in department store catalogs and commercials for Hallmark reading cards and Chuckles candy. "Eddie was a child model."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Child Modeling Career – Department Store Catalogs, Bozo the Clown (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: Growing up in Chicago, Eddie Vedder's mother entered him in photo shoots and TV commercial auditions from a young age. He appeared in at least five department store catalogs modeling back-to-school clothing for five-year-olds. His TV commercial work included spots for Hallmark greeting cards and Chuckles candy. He appeared in a Big Wheel toy commercial that aired during Saturday morning cartoons. His most prominent childhood appearance was on the nationally broadcast *Bozo the Clown* show in the early 1970s. As a grunge icon with serious social, political, and environmental views, this chapter of his life is one he would rather keep quiet. "He would rather not be known as the cute child model for Bloomingdale's."

podcast.title: Early Love for Bootlegs
podcast.body: Eddie Vedder had a personal history with bootlegs, recalling how he would sneak recorders into concerts as a kid to relive the experience at home. This early appreciation likely influenced Pearl Jam's later policy of being bootleg-friendly and their eventual decision to release official bootlegs. "Eddie Vedder remembers sneaking in recorders into shows when he was a kid, just so he could relive the concert experience over and over again at home."

xref.title: Formation Origin - Pickup Basketball Game (1989)
xref.body: The band's genesis began in Seattle when Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament formed Love Company and sought a singer by circulating a demo. Jack Irons, a former Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer, received a copy of this demo and passed it to Eddie Vedder, a surfer and night shift worker at a Chevron tank farm in San Diego, after a pickup basketball game in 1989. Eddie then wrote lyrics to three of the demo's five songs, dubbed them onto a new cassette, and sent it to Seattle, leading to his invitation to jam with the group and the formation of Pearl Jam. "This cassette passed out of a gym bag sometime in 1989 might have resulted in the most profitable pickup basketball game ever played."

xref.title: Bile Beer Drinking Contest – 1992 Lollapalooza, Jim Rose Circus, Matt "the Tube" Crowley
xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would swallow a seven-foot hose connected to a hand pump, force beer, ketchup, mustard, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach, then pump it all back out into glasses for audience members to drink. At one stop on the tour featuring both Pearl Jam and Soundgarden, Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell entered a competition to see who could consume the most of this bile cocktail. Eddie won decisively and named his victory "Wayne." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

xref.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

Eddie Vedder famously won this contest. "And for the record and for all time, Eddie won this contest."

xref.title: Eddie Vedder Stalker (1994–1996) – Believed Eddie Was Jesus and Father of Her Children
xref.body: Between approximately 1994 and 1996, a mentally ill woman became convinced that all of Eddie Vedder's Pearl Jam songs were written personally about her. She also believed that Jesus was the father of her two children via rape, and that Eddie Vedder was Jesus — therefore the father of her children. Physical threats were made, forcing the installation of fences, security systems, and 24-hour bodyguards. Reports indicated she was armed. The situation escalated when she drove her car at 50 mph directly into Eddie's house, at which point he relocated to an inaccessible location outside Seattle. Legal proceedings produced little result. The experience contributed to Eddie's reputation as a recluse and hermit during this period, and is reflected in the song "Lukin" from *No Code* (1996). "Eddie ended up with this reputation as a recluse and a hermit, but now you know why."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. All kinds of people came to pay their respects, including Lemmy of Motorhead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (2000)
xref.body: On June 30, 2000, Pearl Jam performed at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark during its second day, following heavy rains that left 100,000 attendees soaked and safety concerns that led other bands like The Verve and Pet Shop Boys to cancel. During Pearl Jam's 11:30 PM set, a crowd surge pushed attendees against a steel barrier down a slight, muddy incline. Vocalist Eddie Vedder repeatedly stopped the band, imploring the crowd to move back as the crush became a "slow-motion avalanche of bodies." Ultimately, 26 people were injured, and 8 bodies were pulled from the pile, with another person dying later in hospital. The victims were from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden. "Our lives will never be the same, but we know that this is nothing compared to the grief of the families and friends of those involved."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Roskilde Festival Tragedy (June 30, 2000)
xref.body: On Friday, June 30, 2000, during Pearl Jam's performance at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark, a crowd surge towards the stage led to a catastrophic crush. Despite Eddie Vedder and the band pleading with the audience to move back, nine people died and countless others were injured when a customized padded barrier failed. This event became one of Europe's worst concert tragedies, leading to the cancellation of the rest of the festival and a police investigation. Pearl Jam fully cooperated, was exonerated from criminal charges, but seriously considered quitting the band due to immense guilt. "nine people died in the crush and countless other suffered injuries making it one of Europe's worst ever concert tragedies."

xref.title: Performance on Vote for Change Tour (2004)
xref.body: Eddie Vedder was invited on stage by Bruce Springsteen to perform "Better Man" during a last-minute added New Jersey show on October 13, 2004, as part of the "Vote for Change Tour," an event dedicated to influencing the 2004 US presidential election. "A New Jersey show was added at the last second on October the 13th, 2004. And Midway through the gig, Springsteen invited Eddie Vetteron stage to play Better Man."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Eddie Vedder's Reflection on Roskilde (June 27, 2007)
xref.body: On June 27, 2007, in Copenhagen, Eddie Vedder spoke about the Roskilde tragedy seven years later, acknowledging that the event affected not just the band but their entire "family," including their long-time crew and the friends and relatives of the victims present. He expressed the profound honor of their presence and reflected on the absence of "closure," instead finding strength and healing in collective remembrance and understanding of loss. "Eddie Vetter has addressed the Ross Killed tragedy several times. This is from June 27, 2007 in Copenhagen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Eddie Vedder's Return to Copenhagen (2007)
xref.body: On June 27, 2007, seven years after the Roskilde tragedy, Pearl Jam played at the Forum in Copenhagen. Eddie Vedder addressed the crowd from the stage, speaking about the impossibility of "closure" but the importance of connecting and learning from the loss. He specifically acknowledged the family of Frank Noens, one of the men who died at Roskilde, noting his mother Antoinette, sister Kathy, and friends were in attendance to celebrate his life, as a request from Kathy. "And I said, no, there's no closure. Is that the word in English? There's no closure. There's no end of the street."

xref.title: Brian's Junior High Shooting Incident
xref.body: One of the inspirations for "Jeremy" came from Eddie Vedder's own junior high experience in San Diego during the 1970s. A troubled seventh-grader named Brian, with whom Vedder had some confrontations, brought a sawed-off shotgun to school, hid it in bushes until lunchtime, and then shot up a 1,000-gallon fish tank. Although no one was injured or died, the event deeply shook Vedder, prompting him to consider what if he had been in the fish tank room at that moment. "No one died, no one was injured. But I mentioned that kind of thing happening in an elementary school back in the 1970s."

"Most of the musicians who took part in the Temple of the Dog Sessions really had a good time hanging out. And when the record was finished, Mother Love Bone's bassist and guitarist decided to stick together."

xref.title: Eddie Vedder Was a Child Model – Department Store Catalogs, TV Commercials, Bozo the Clown
xref.body: Growing up in Chicago, Eddie's mother entered him in photo shoots and TV commercial auditions. He appeared in at least five department store catalogs (including Bloomingdale's) modeling back-to-school clothing as a five-year-old, and appeared in TV commercials for Hallmark greeting cards and Chuckles candy. He was one of the kids driving a Big Wheel in a commercial that ran during Saturday morning cartoons. His biggest triumph was an appearance on the nationally broadcast *Bozo the Clown* show in the early 1970s. "He would rather not be known as the cute child model for Bloomingdale's."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Eddie Vedder's Audition Tape Creation
xref.body: After receiving a demo tape from Jack Irons, Eddie Vedder listened to it repeatedly. Following a night shift and a surfing session, he sat down at home and wrote lyrics for three of the five songs on the tape. He then recorded his vocals and the new lyrics onto a cassette and mailed it to Seattle, where Jeff Ament and Stone Gossard immediately recognized his talent, solidifying his role as their frontman. "As soon as Eddie got the tape from Jack, he started listening to it over and over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fanbase
xref.body: The Vandals enjoyed a notable fanbase among prominent figures in alternative rock, including Kurt Cobain and Eddie Vedder, indicating their influence and appeal within the wider rock community. "Kurt Cobain was a fan of the vandals, and so is Eddie Vetter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Father's Anguish Over "Jeremy"
xref.body: After Pearl Jam's song "Jeremy" became a hit, reporters tracked down Jeremy Dell's father, Joseph Dell. He expressed profound anguish over the song's impact, describing how fans often leave notes and artifacts at Jeremy's grave, and how numerous websites, frequented by young teenagers, romanticize his son's suicide, often displaying adoration for Eddie Vedder. Joseph Dell's letter highlights the pain caused by the song's glorification of the act. "My anguish is just as deep with each call, note or email."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First to Release Music
xref.body: Harper was the first of Eddie Vedder's daughters to release music, contributing a cover song with her father to the launch of a Pearl Jam-dedicated Sirius XM channel in 2016. "Harper was the first to release some music when Sirius XM launched a channel dedicated to Pearl Jam in 2016."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation from Mother Love Bone and Temple of the Dog
xref.body: Pearl Jam was formed by Mother Love Bone's bassist Jeff Ament and guitarist Stone Gossard, who decided to continue playing together after the Temple of the Dog sessions. They were joined by guitarist Mike McCready, a veteran of several small Seattle groups, and singer Eddie Vedder, who had moved from San Diego to perform background vocals on the Temple of the Dog record. "Jeff Ammett and Stone Gossard were joined by guitarist Mike McCready, a veteran of several small Seattle groups. And for a singer, they chose this skinny surfer dude who had moved up from San Diego to do background vocals on the Temple of the Dog record. His name was Eddie Vetter and the result of course was Pearl Jam."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Friendships with Notable Musicians and Figures
xref.body: Mark Lanegan was close friends with Chef Anthony Bourdain, for whom he wrote an obituary, as well as Layne Staley of Alice in Chains, Eddie Vedder, the members of Soundgarden, and Kurt Cobain. "He was also good friends with Chef Anthony Bourdain. He wrote an obituary on Bourdain when he died. He was also buddies with doomed Ellison Chainsinger, Lane Staley. Other friends included Eddie Vedder, all the guys in Soundgarden and Kurt Cobain."

xref.title: Jack Irons' Collaboration – During Matt Cameron's Soundgarden Tenure
xref.body: Jack Irons, who was once a drummer for Eleven and briefly for the Red Hot Chili Peppers, worked with Pearl Jam at a time when Matt Cameron was performing with Soundgarden. Irons also played a crucial role in Eddie Vedder joining the band by passing along a demo tape. "Jack would later join the Red Hot Chili Peppers for a bit, and he worked with Pearl Jam when Matt Cameron went off with Soundgarden."

xref.title: Members' Future Bands
xref.body: After the Temple of the Dog album was released, Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron were active in Soundgarden, while Stone Gossard, Jeff Ament, Mike McCready, and Eddie Vedder formed Pearl Jam. "By the time that Temple of Dog album came out, Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron were doing well in Soundgarden, while the other guys in the group stayed together in Formed Pearl Jam."

xref.title: Musical Collaboration with Father
xref.body: Olivia has been working on music with her father, Eddie Vedder, for some time. "Olivia Vetter has been working with Dad on music for a while now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Naming Fictional Band "Citizen Dick"
xref.body: Jeff Ament was tasked with coming up with a name for a fictional band that he, Eddie Vedder, Stone Gossard, and actor Matt Dillon would be part of in the movie *Singles*. From his list of options, "Citizen Dick" was selected as the winning name. "Jeff Amit had been given the task of coming up with a name for a fictional band that he, Eddie and Stone and Matt Dillon, one of the stars of the film, would be in, so he listed a bunch of options."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nirvana Dissolution if Alive
xref.body: Speculation suggests that if Kurt had lived, Nirvana might have dissolved undramatically, with Kurt pursuing his non-grunge, acoustic musical ideas, similar to later unplugged shows by Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell. "maybe he would just sort of dissolve Nirvana. Not a breakup, but just an undramatic fade to black."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pearl Jam Fan Community Bootlegs
xref.body: Despite their unreleased album, the Pearl Jam fan community has actively kept Bad Radio's music alive by circulating bootlegs of their material. This effort by fans ensures that the music from Eddie Vedder's pre-Pearl Jam band remains accessible. "Meanwhile, the Pearl Jam fan community has kept Bad Radio alive by circulating boot legs of Bad Radio stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Perceived Feud with Nirvana
xref.body: Pearl Jam was initially viewed critically by Kurt Cobain, who considered them "careerists," too commercial, corporate, and appealing to "jocks." However, Kurt later clarified that the perceived feud was largely his fault and that he should have targeted the record company for pushing Pearl Jam onto the "grunge bandwagon" without their full realization or will. Eddie Vedder now agrees with Kurt's assessment of what was happening to Pearl Jam at the time. "That never was a feud. I slagged them off because I didn't like their band. It was my fault. I should have been slagging off the record company instead of them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Predecessor to Pearl Jam – Formation with Eddie Vedder
xref.body: Mookie Blaylock was the original name of the band formed by Mother Love Bone's Jeff Ament and Stone Gossard, who invited a young singer named Eddie Vedder from San Diego to join. The band quickly changed its name to Pearl Jam, which went on to achieve massive success. "This kid from San Diego who had just flown up at the invitation of Jeff and Stone to sing in a new band that was going to be called Mookie Blaylock, and that kid's name was Eddie Vedder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers Sound Shift
xref.body: After Eddie Vedder became their singer, Bad Radio's sound evolved to become increasingly similar to that of the Red Hot Chili Peppers. "After Eddie came on board, Bad Radio began to sound more and more like the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rediscovery by Grunge Bands
xref.body: In the early 1990s, new Grunge bands, notably led by Kurt Cobain and Eddie Vedder, began publicly praising The Ramones, "name-checking" them and wearing their t-shirts, which initiated a rediscovery of the band by a new generation of fans. "All these new bands, led by kids like Kirk Cobain and Eddie Better, started name-checking the Ramones. They were seen wearing Ramones t-shirts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Response to Grunge Label
xref.body: Scott Weiland intensely disliked being compared to grunge bands, particularly Pearl Jam and Eddie Vedder. He felt that the obvious differences in his fashion sense and stage presence, which lacked any flannel, should have distinguished them. To counter these criticisms, Weiland deliberately adopted a more flamboyant, performance art aspect to his stagecraft, incorporating dresses, lipstick, and mascara. "There was certainly no flannel in Scott's wardrobe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Support from Indie Musicians
xref.body: Indie musicians in Chicago and beyond, including producer Steve Albini and a former bandmate of Billy Corgan from a pre-Smashing Pumpkins band, took notice and supported Wesley. The Canadian industrial metal band Monster Voodoo Machine recorded with him, and Eddie Vedder was charmed by his work. "The indie musicians of Chicago and beyond took note, and they took a liking to him."

xref.title: Transformation into Pearl Jam – Post-Tragedy Rebirth
xref.body: Following the tragic death of Andrew Wood, the surviving members of Mother Love Bone, Jeff Ament and Stone Gossard, collaborated with Chris Cornell and Matt Cameron to form Temple of the Dog. This collaboration eventually led Ament and Gossard to form a new band with Eddie Vedder, initially called Mookie Blaylock, which soon became Pearl Jam. "When Mother Lovebone collapsed and turned into Pearl Jam, Kelly became their full-time manager, leaving Susan to deal with Allison Chains."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Vocal Style Development
xref.body: Ben, the vocalist, initially spent the first five years of the band trying to emulate other singers like Eddie Vedder, Scott Weiland, and Zack de la Rocha. He eventually realized he couldn't sound like them and developed his own distinctive style. This unique vocal approach, combined with Ian's guitar playing, helped the band stand out from other Canadian bands of the era like Moist, Treble Charger, and The Tea Party. "I, the first five years of being in a band, you know, I was trying to sound like other people, you know, I was trying to sound like Eddie Vetter. I was trying to sound like Scott Watt. I'm trying to sound like Zack Delroch. You know, like, I'm trying to do that. And then I realized I can't do that, you know, so I just kind of ended up being me."
